steps.name: Your vector
steps.question: Can you name the one role you are going for, the kind of company, and a date?
levels: I am open to anything interesting.
I can name the next role.
Role, kind of company and a date, written down and said out loud to at least two people.
steps.why: Every later step is built on it: the title, the pitch, the list of companies.
steps.skip: The pitch lies, the network calls are vague, the interviews wander.

steps.name: Your title and your number
steps.question: Does your headline combine a business domain with a technical scope, and do you know your number?
levels: My headline is my current job title, often with a programming language. I have no number.
A role-based title, and a salary range in my head.
Domain plus scope on LinkedIn and the CV (Team Lead becomes Fintech Engineering Manager), and one number I can defend with evidence.
steps.why: The title is the first thing a recruiter, a CTO or their AI reads. The number decides where the negotiation starts.
steps.skip: You anchor low, or you dodge the question.

steps.name: Your dream companies
steps.question: Do you have a written list of 10 to 15 companies where a CTO or VP could hire you?
levels: I apply to what is posted.
I have some names in my head.
10 to 15 names written down, filtered by product or deep tech, size, hybrid or remote and country. I know who decides at five of them.
steps.why: A list turns a job search into a plan you can work through the network.
steps.skip: You apply everywhere and hear back from few.

steps.name: Your one-minute pitch
steps.question: Can you say your largest outcome, your differentiator and your potential in one minute?
levels: I recite my CV.
I can introduce myself in a minute.
Largest outcome, differentiator, potential. Rehearsed, and it makes the other person ask a question.
steps.why: Every coffee, intro and interview opens with it.
steps.skip: If you can't sell yourself in one minute, nobody listens for the other 59.

steps.name: Your digital footprint
steps.question: What does someone find when they look you up?
levels: A LinkedIn timeline of job titles. No public work.
LinkedIn updated with outcomes.
LinkedIn with the new title and proof, plus GitHub with a pet project or an AI skill other people use.
steps.why: The person who recommends you, and the one who hires you, open your profile first.
steps.skip: Nothing there, and the recommendation ends at the first question.

steps.name: Your network
steps.question: How many people who have seen your work would vouch for you to a CTO?
levels: My current colleagues.
About 20 people would take my call.
I listed 50, reactivated 10 this quarter, and 10 would vouch for me.
steps.why: The best roles are taken through the network before anyone writes the ad.
steps.skip: In five years, with no connections, your options will suck.

steps.name: Be heard
steps.question: How often do you speak or publish outside your company?
levels: I have not spoken or published outside my company.
One talk, podcast or post a year, and I belong to a community.
Three or more public appearances a year: a meetup, a podcast, a conference.
steps.why: Speaking, presenting and communication are priced skills, and they put you in front of the people who decide.
steps.skip: The roles go to peers who are louder, not better.

steps.name: Your AI level
steps.question: Which of the five AI levels describes your week: Ask, Brief, Repeat, Connect, Supervise?
levels: Level 1 or 2: I ask and I brief.
Level 3: saved prompts or skills I reuse every week.
Level 4 or 5: AI acts in my tools, or runs a process under rules I wrote.
steps.why: Someone who ships with AI daily is scarce in a market where nearly everyone claims to.
steps.skip: You sit next to the AI and watch it work.

steps.name: Outcomes, not outputs
steps.question: When you describe your work, do you say what you did or what changed?
levels: Projects, deadlines, tasks.
A few outcome statements with numbers.
Thirty or more outcome statements, and the outcome words come out by themselves, also under pressure.
steps.why: Leaders buy outcomes: product, impact, mission, value.
steps.skip: Your work is a nine and it lands like a five.

steps.name: B-list first, then A-list
steps.question: Do you practise on the companies you could live without before you talk to the ones you want?
levels: I would go straight to my dream company.
I know which are practice and which are targets.
I finish B-list conversations before any A-list one.
steps.why: The first conversations are the worst ones. Spend them where they cost nothing.
steps.skip: You burn your dream company on your worst interview.

steps.name: Interview dry runs
steps.question: How many recorded dry runs have you done with someone who hires?
levels: None.
One mock interview with a friend.
Three or more, recorded, with feedback from someone who hires.
steps.why: A real interview is not the place to find your weak spots.
steps.skip: You get the meeting and then you freeze.

steps.name: Negotiate, then protect your first months
steps.question: Do you negotiate with evidence, and do you have a plan for your first 3 to 6 months?
levels: I take the first offer and start.
I ask for more, and I think about the first weeks.
An anchor with evidence, silence after it, a walk-away I mean, and a written 30-60-90 day plan.
steps.why: Negotiation is a thirty-minute skill that pays for about a decade, and the first months decide whether you keep the job.
steps.skip: You take the first offer out of relief.
